title: Fluids
scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT Physics, Mathematics and Research Reasoning lessons. Models and calculations use stated assumptions. Independent scientific review is pending; this is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: Density is mass per volume. Pressure is force per area, while viscosity characterizes resistance to shear flow; these are different properties.
A fluid at rest does not sustain a static shear stress like an elastic solid. Liquids and gases flow under sustained shear, although their compressibilities differ.
A nearly incompressible liquid model holds density approximately fixed. Treating a gas this way requires a justified regime rather than a universal assumption.
Viscosity influences flow resistance and dissipation. A denser fluid is not necessarily more viscous; compare measured or stated properties separately.

steps.text: For a static liquid of uniform density, pressure at depth h is Psurface + ρgh. Gauge pressure subtracts the chosen reference atmospheric pressure.
At the same depth in one connected static fluid, pressure is equal. Vessel shape does not alter the hydrostatic depth contribution under these assumptions.
Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid. It depends on submerged volume and fluid density, not automatically on the entire object’s weight.
A floating object has buoyancy balancing its weight in static equilibrium. For a fully submerged object, compare density and other forces before predicting motion.

steps.text: For steady incompressible flow through an unbranched tube, continuity gives A1v1 = A2v2. A smaller area requires a larger mean flow speed at the same volume flow rate.
Bernoulli’s relation P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant applies along a streamline for steady incompressible flow with negligible viscous losses and no intervening pump work.
For laminar Newtonian flow in a long cylindrical tube, Poiseuille resistance is 8ηL/(πr⁴). Radius changes have a fourth-power effect only within this model’s assumptions.
Real vascular flow can be pulsatile, branched and dissipative. Do not apply a frictionless constant-Bernoulli sum across every real vessel or a pressure-adding pump.

steps.text: A useful circulation model relates volume flow to driving pressure difference divided by resistance: Qflow = ΔP/R. Volume flow is not the same quantity as local speed.
Parallel vessels can have a large combined area, lowering average speed for a given total flow. Narrowing one vessel differs from distributing flow across many small vessels.
A simplified cylindrical-vessel model predicts strong radius sensitivity, but real blood is cellular and vessels can change diameter. State assumptions before using a rigid Newtonian-tube equation.
Conservation of flow applies at junctions: total inflow equals total outflow in steady conditions. Physiological variation and compliance can make instantaneous flows differ from steady averages.
